title: Forecasting-driven provisioner and surge shepherding for embeddings
creator: Avery Chen
description:
Problem: Embeddings endpoints experience short, high-concurrency surges from a small set of tenants which cause queue growth, p99 latency spikes, and upstream throttling. Current autoscaler reacts too slowly to 1-5 minute spikes and doesn't account for warm KV cache or per-tenant headroom. We need an approach that: (a) predicts short-term demand and pre-provisions capacity, (b) protects steady-state latency SLOs during bursts by admission control and graceful degradation, and (c) keeps unit costs bounded with intelligent warm-pool sizing and pre-warming policies.

Scope: Design and implement a forecasting-driven provisioner + "surge shepherd" admission controller for the embeddings service. Covers: forecasting model, admission control policy, warm-pool sizing, per-tenant headroom accounting, metrics/telemetry changes, integration with Dedicated capacity planner, and rollout strategy. Does NOT include embedding model accuracy changes or embedding model quantization (separate work).
acceptance_criteria:
- Forecasting pipeline runs on 1-min cadence and produces per-tenant 1/5/15-minute demand forecasts and a global cluster headroom recommendation.
- Autoscaler uses forecasts to start warm instances at least 30s before predicted surge 80% of the time in the test harness.
- Admission controller enforces per-tenant burst tokens and declines non-critical low-priority requests instead of inflating p99.
- End-to-end integration maintains p50 < 40ms and p99 < 220ms for embeddings synthetic workload with 10x spike tests vs baseline where p99 was >600ms.
- Dashboards surfaced in Console with queue depth, forecasted headroom, warm pool utilization, and rejected-request ratio.
- PRs merged, infra migration runbook updated, and canary rollout executed with no Sev >P2 incidents.
design_notes:
Proposal summary:
1) Forecasting: lightweight time-series ensemble (exponential smoothing + short-window median + anomaly dampening). Runs in a separate forecasting service that subscribes to per-tenant QPS and queue-depth streams. Outputs: tenant_forecast_{1m,5m,15m} and cluster_headroom_recommendation.
2) Provisioner: a controller that converts cluster_headroom_recommendation into requested warm instances. It interacts with pool manager to create warm VMs/containers with KV cache warming hooks. Keep minimal lifecycle: pre-warm -> standby -> serve -> cool-down.
3) Admission controller ("Surge Shepherd"): enforces token buckets per-tenant and global burst budget. Low-priority calls (batch/async embedding jobs) are queued to a best-effort lane; high-priority interactive requests get preferential tokens. When near capacity, controller declines or redirects low-priority work to a fallback embedding model (smaller/different quantization) to preserve p99.
4) Headroom accounting: per-tenant reserved slots tracked in Redis summary table; ephemeral reservations for in-flight batching.
5) Observability: new telemetry keys (forecast_delta, warm_pool_fill, reserve_leak_count). Add alerts: forecast_vs_actual > 200% for 2 windows, warm_pool_miss_rate > 10%.

Engineering trade-offs considered:
- Use simple forecasting to avoid model ops overhead; heavier models gave small incremental accuracy at high ops cost.
- Start with container-level warm pools rather than cross-tenant cache sharing to limit blast radius.
- Admission controller implemented in the router layer to minimize changes to runtime.

Open questions:
- Warm-cache warming strategy per model variant (how many tokens to pre-populate?). Proposed default: seed KV with recent popular prefixes (from hot-keys telemetry).
- How to price reserved headroom for Dedicated customers? Product to define billing approach.
rollout_plan:
1) Feature flag gated: forecasting+provisioner OFF by default.
2) Unit tests + integration tests in staging with synthetic spike harness.
3) Canary A: enable forecasting signals (read-only) for 10% of tenants to validate forecast accuracy (2 days).
4) Canary B: enable provisioner for non-critical pools (no customer-impact) and verify warm instance creation (3 days).
5) Canary C: enable admission controller in shadow mode for 48h; compare decisions vs baseline.
6) Soft launch: enable for 5% of traffic to measure p99 impact and rejected-request ratio (7 days).
7) Ramp to 100% with gradual config tuning.
8) Post-launch: 14-day telemetry review and rollback window.

Rollback criteria: sustained p99 increase > 30% or decline in successful request rate > 5% for 30m.
metrics:
Primary: embeddings_p99_latency_ms, embeddings_p50_latency_ms, queue_depth_per_pool, forecast_error_1m_pct, warm_pool_utilization_pct, rejected_request_ratio, warm_pool_start_time_s, provisioner_lag_s.
SLO targets: embeddings_p99 < 220ms, rejected_request_ratio < 0.5% overall.
Dashboards: Console route-level view + tenant-level heatmap for forecast accuracy.
testing_plan:
- Add synthetic spike harness that can simulate 1k tenants with independent diurnal and bursty patterns.
- Load tests: 10x and 20x short spikes (30s-3m) and long spikes (10-30m). Validate forecast lead time and warm-start success.
- Chaos tests: kill warm nodes mid-spike to test fallback behavior.
- Regression tests: ensure embeddings correctness unchanged; run existing embedding e2e suites.
- Canary monitoring: automated smoke checks and latency guardians.
risks:
- Forecast underprediction could cause late starts and p99 spikes (mitigation: conservative multiplier + emergency reactive autoscaling).
- Over-provisioning increases cost (mitigation: warm_pool timeouts, aggressive cool-down, cost dashboard).
- Complexity in per-tenant accounting might create edge conditions causing denied critical requests (mitigation: safe-list critical tenants; shadow mode).
- Integration with Dedicated reserved pools requires contract/product alignment (mitigation: gated feature for Dedicated until billing decision made).
